draft.title: An industrial process
card: The Haber process makes ammonia: N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g). The forward reaction is exothermic and 4 mol of gas become 2 mol.
By Le Chatelier's principle, a lower temperature and a higher pressure shift the equilibrium towards ammonia. This raises the yield at equilibrium.
A low temperature makes the reaction too slow. So industry uses a moderately high temperature, around 400 to 500 °C, with an iron-based catalyst to raise the rate.
Very high pressure gives a better yield but needs costly equipment and more energy. So a high but not extreme pressure is used. Ammonia is removed as a liquid and unreacted gases are recycled.
draft.remember: An industrial process is a compromise: conditions are chosen to balance rate, yield and cost.

a.q: Why is the Haber process run at about 400 to 500 °C and not at a much lower temperature?
opts: The reaction would be too slow
The yield at equilibrium would fall
The catalyst would stop working at all
The forward reaction would turn endothermic
a.why: Lowering the temperature favours the exothermic forward reaction, so the equilibrium yield would rise. But the rate becomes too slow to be useful, so a moderately high temperature is a compromise. The yield does not fall at lower temperatures.
a.clue: Think about what low temperature does to rate, not yield.

b.q: A plant makes ammonia by the Haber process. Its engineers raise the pressure from 200 atm to a much higher value. Which is the most likely drawback?
opts: Equipment and energy costs rise sharply
The equilibrium shifts away from ammonia
The catalyst is used up in the reaction
The forward reaction becomes endothermic
b.why: Very high pressure needs stronger, costlier equipment and more energy to compress the gases. Higher pressure still shifts the equilibrium towards ammonia, because fewer gas moles are on the product side, so the yield is not the problem.
b.clue: Higher pressure helps the yield. What might it cost?

a.best: The reaction would be too slow

b.best: Equipment and energy costs rise sharply
